problems.source_says: The Study 3 method names no generative-AI tool. The only AI in it gives 'investment advice' in a modified trust game on decision-making problems, and the paper does not say what kind of AI this is (a language model or anything else). For Phase 3 the text says only that the AUT was 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2'. Section 4 never mentions ChatGPT and never says whether any arm had an AI tool during the AUT. So generative_ai for these arms is an inference from Study 2, not a statement about Study 3.

problems.source_says: Nothing in Study 3 says that participants used a chatbot. open_chat assumes that the Study 2 ChatGPT setup carried over to the Study 3 AUT. The nearest text is in the General Discussion, which says the Study 3 effect 'does not require complete AI abstinence' and speaks of shifting the 'usage style' from outcome- to process-oriented. That 'usage style' is the thinking-orientation prime, and the sentence does not say that ChatGPT was available during the AUT. The name_model text ('Not stated for Study 3') is accurate. The supplement's task instructions for Study 3, which are not in this PDF, may settle the point.

problems.source_says: The Study 3 high and low AI-dependence arms differ in one instruction given in a trust game on decision problems before the creative task: trust the AI's advice, or use autonomous judgment. The paper does not say that the arms used AI differently on the AUT, or that AI was available on the AUT at all. The limitations paragraph says high-dependence participants 'were explicitly told to adopt AI outputs' after naming 'the experimental manipulations in Studies 2 and 3', which fits the trust game as well as an AUT instruction. If the AUT ran without AI, or with the same AI instructions in every arm, the arms differ only in an earlier trust-game prime, which is not random assignment to generative-AI assistance on a creative task. The form's measure_detail and open_questions call AI availability inferred, and eligibility.reason calls criterion 1 unclear for Study 3, but these coded values present the inference as fact.
problems.quote: Phase 1 involved the AI dependence manipulation, using a modified trust game paradigm (Klingbeil et al., 2024): participants faced a series of decision-making problems

confirmed.statement: (a) Study 2 states random assignment: 132 students 'were recruited and randomly assigned to either the high-dependence group (n = 66) or the low-dependence group (n = 66).' The form's quote is verbatim, and the 66 + 66 arm counts match. The paper does not describe how the randomization was done. It says the groups did not differ in age, gender, or disciplinary background.

(e) Study 2 is between-subjects, so order randomization does not apply: 'Study 2 employed a single-factor between-subjects experimental design'. Each student is assigned to one group, which supports unit = individual and structure = between. The paper mentions no clustered or session-level assignment.
confirmed.locator: p. 5, Section 3.1, Objective, and Section 3.2, Participants

confirmed.statement: (b) Study 2 assigned each participant's own use of ChatGPT. In Phase 1 the high group had to 'strictly use ChatGPT-generated answers' for three tasks, told that 'the answers provided by the AI are optimal'. The low group did the same tasks 'without using any external tools, including calculators, translation applications, search engines, or AI assistance'. In Phase 2 'participants in both groups used ChatGPT' on the AUT. The high group was told to 'directly adopt the creative solutions generated by ChatGPT', and the low group to 'use AI only as a supplementary reference and to independently complete their final solutions'. Each participant submits their own AUT response, so the conditions do not differ only in whose output is rated. By instruction, the high arm submits ChatGPT's solutions, which the form flags (open_questions, item 5).
confirmed.locator: pp. 5-6, Section 3.2, Experimental design and procedure

confirmed.statement: (c) The Study 2 tool is generative AI. The paper lists ChatGPT among 'Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools' and names ChatGPT as the tool in both phases. No model version appears anywhere in the document, so 'ChatGPT (model version not stated)' is right. open_chat fits: participants used ChatGPT themselves, in a full-screen browser lockdown with an experimenter present, and the paper does not describe their prompts.
confirmed.locator: p. 1, Introduction, first paragraph; p. 5, Section 3.2, Experimental design and procedure

confirmed.statement: (d) The Study 2 comparison arm matches the form (another AI configuration, ai_design). Both arms used ChatGPT on the AUT under different instructions. The arms also differ in the Phase 1 prime (mandatory ChatGPT answers vs no tools), as the form records. One sentence says participants heard the no-tools prohibition 'again before the creativity task in Phase 2', which conflicts with 'participants in both groups used ChatGPT'. The form flags this (notes, item 10) and follows the two explicit Phase 2 statements. Under either reading the arms differ in generative-AI assistance, so criterion 1 holds.

confirmed.statement: Full-text search: the only statements of random assignment are on p. 5 (Study 2) and p. 7 (Study 3). The other 'random' hit is the rater sheets, 'presented in random order' (p. 6). ChatGPT appears on p. 1 (introduction), pp. 5-6 (Study 2 method), and p. 11 (a teaching example), never in Section 4 (Study 3).

summary: Study 2 supports the conclusion: the paper states that 132 students were randomly assigned (p. 5) to two between-subjects arms that differ in ChatGPT use, first mandatory ChatGPT answers versus no tools in a priming phase, then 'directly adopt' ChatGPT's AUT solutions versus use AI 'only as a supplementary reference', so criterion 1 holds for the paper. The Study 3 coding is not supported: its random assignment (p. 7) is to a trust-game instruction about unnamed 'AI’s investment advice' crossed with a thinking-orientation prime, and the text never says that ChatGPT or any generative AI was available on its AUT, so the arms' generative_ai value, the open_chat role, and the ai_design contrasts for Study 3 rest only on 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2'.
